why.correct: W shows separate ions in a 1 : 1 ratio, with water's δ− oxygen toward Na⁺ and a δ+ hydrogen toward Cl⁻.
options: Right: separate ions, 1 : 1, correct orientation.
X has every water molecule backwards: H toward the cation and O toward the anion, so like charges face each other.
Y shows the ions still paired, but dissolving separates them into hydrated ions.
Z shows two Na⁺ for one Cl⁻, which has a net charge of +1 and the wrong ratio for NaCl.

why.correct: Ion-dipole attraction lines up opposite charges. X turns every water molecule backwards, which would put repelling charges side by side.
options: Right: the orientation is reversed for both ions.
Dissolving does separate the ions; that part of X is correct.
Each ion is surrounded by several water molecules, so a shell of four is reasonable.
Cl⁻ (181 pm) is larger than Na⁺ (102 pm), as drawn.

why.correct: Ion-dipole attractions pull the ions out of the lattice and apart. A correct drawing shows each ion separately, with its own water shell.
options: Right: the ions should be separate and hydrated.
Y shows several water molecules; the number drawn is a sampling choice.
NaCl gives a 1 : 1 ratio, which Y gets right.
The O–H bonds in water do not break when salt dissolves.

why.correct: NaCl is 1 : 1, so any box of NaCl(aq) has equal numbers of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ and a total charge of zero.
options: Right: the formula ratio, and the charge balance, are wrong.
Cations are hydrated too, with water's O pointing in.
A solution is homogeneous, so ions spread through it.
NaCl is ionic and separates into ions.

why.correct: Three SO₄²⁻ ions and six K⁺ ions: 3 + 6 = 9 ions. Each sulfate ion counts as one particle; its atoms stay bonded together.
The formula K₂SO₄ fixes the ratio: two K⁺ per SO₄²⁻, which makes each formula unit, and the whole box, neutral.
options: Right: the ratio follows the formula and the charges.
Ion size does not set how many of each ion form.
Sulfate stays whole; the S–O bonds are covalent.
Every formula unit gives the same two K⁺ and one SO₄²⁻.

why.correct: Opposite charges face each other: water's δ− oxygen toward the cation, and its δ+ hydrogens toward the negatively charged sulfate ion (whose outer O atoms carry the negative charge).
options: Right: δ− to the cation, δ+ to the anion.
This reverses both: like charges would face each other.
Atom size does not decide; charge does, and O is δ− so it suits only the cation.
H is δ+, so it is attracted to the anion but repelled by the cation.

why.correct: Each K₂SO₄ gives two K⁺, so [K⁺] = 2 × 0.150 M = 0.300 M.
By Coulomb's law the attraction grows with charge and falls with distance. Mg²⁺ has the larger charge (2+) and the smallest radius, so water molecules can get closest to the most charge.
options: K⁺ has a 1+ charge and the largest radius.
Na⁺ has only a 1+ charge and a larger radius than Mg²⁺.
Ca²⁺ has the same charge as Mg²⁺ but a larger radius, so water sits farther away.
Right: high charge, small radius.

why.correct: Glucose is a molecular compound. It dissolves as intact molecules held among the water molecules by hydrogen bonds; it forms no ions.
options: Right: intact molecules, evenly spread.
Dissolving does not break covalent bonds; the molecules stay whole.
Glucose is not ionic and does not form ions.
A solution is homogeneous, so the molecules spread evenly.

why.correct: Ca(NO₃)₂ → Ca²⁺ + 2 NO₃⁻. Nitrate ions stay whole, the ions spread evenly, and water's oxygen (not hydrogen) points at Ca²⁺.
options: Right: the formula ratio is 1 : 2.
Right: polyatomic ions keep their covalent bonds.
Water's δ+ hydrogens would be repelled by a cation; the oxygen points in.
Nitrate stays whole when the salt dissolves.
Right: a solution is homogeneous.
Dissolving separates the ions; they do not stay as formula units.

why.correct: Ion-dipole attraction is Coulombic. A δ− oxygen is attracted to a cation and repelled by an anion, so around Br⁻ the water molecules turn their δ+ hydrogens inward.
options: Right: orientation depends on the ion's sign.
Ion-dipole forces are not hydrogen bonds, and O–to–anion would repel.
A full charge of either sign attracts the opposite end of water, which differs for + and −.
δ+ H would be repelled by K⁺.

why.correct: AlCl₃ → Al³⁺ + 3 Cl⁻ gives 4 ions per formula unit (0.80 M of particles). NaCl and MgSO₄ give 2 each (0.40 M), and sucrose gives 1 molecule (0.20 M).
options: Sucrose stays as whole molecules: one particle each.
Two ions per formula unit.
Mg²⁺ and SO₄²⁻: two ions per formula unit.
Right: four ions per formula unit.

why.correct: FeCl₃ → Fe³⁺ + 3 Cl⁻, so there is one Fe³⁺ per three Cl⁻: 12 ÷ 3 = 4 Fe³⁺. Check: 4(+3) + 12(−1) = 0.
In the solid the ions are fixed in place. Dissolving separates them into hydrated ions that can move, and moving charged particles carry a current.
options: Right: mobile ions carry the current.
KCl is ionic, not covalent, and no free electrons are released.
Water stays as H₂O molecules; the ions come from the KCl.
The ions separate rather than staying together as KCl units.

why.correct: Rf = 6.4 cm ÷ 8.0 cm = 0.80. The distances share units, so Rf has none.
The drink's spots have Rf = 6.4/8.0 = 0.80 and 2.0/8.0 = 0.25, matching Dye A (0.80) and Dye C (0.25).
options: Right: Rf 0.80 matches.
Dye B has Rf 0.50; the drink has no spot there.
Right: Rf 0.25 matches.
Dye D has Rf 0.15; the drink has no spot there.

why.correct: A small Rf means the component spent most of its time attached to the stationary phase. That reflects stronger attractions to the paper than to the solvent.
options: Right: held most by the stationary phase.
Separation follows attractions to the two phases, not mass.
Strong attraction to the solvent would carry it farther, giving a large Rf.
All samples develop together for the same time.

why.correct: Ink is itself a mixture of dyes and would travel with the solvent, producing spots that could be mistaken for parts of the drink. Pencil (graphite) does not move.
options: Right: the line's own dyes would separate.
Solvent crosses an ink line easily.
The ink line is in the solvent's path and would move with it.
Rf uses measured distances; ink does not change them systematically.

why.correct: Polar dyes are attracted to the polar paper. A less polar solvent attracts them less, so they spend more time on the paper and travel a smaller fraction of the solvent distance.
options: Right: less competition from the solvent, smaller Rf.
Rf is a ratio, so speed does not raise it; attractions decide.
Rf depends on the pair of phases; changing the solvent changes it.
Polar dyes would be held back, not swept to the front.

why.correct: The vapor stays near 56–61 °C for the first 30 mL: that is acetone, the lower-boiling liquid, vaporizing first.
options: Water comes over later, at the 100 °C plateau.
Right: the first plateau is near acetone's boiling point.
The two plateaus show they come over one after the other.
Liquid starts collecting at 56 °C.

why.correct: Acetone has dipole-dipole and dispersion forces but cannot hydrogen-bond to itself; water hydrogen-bonds extensively. Weaker attractions give acetone the higher vapor pressure and the lower boiling point.
options: Right: weaker attractions, more volatile.
Heavier molecules would not escape more easily; and attractions, not mass, decide.
Water molecules stay intact; no covalent bonds break.
Acetone has no H bonded to O, so it cannot hydrogen-bond with itself.

why.correct: The vapor stays near acetone's boiling point until about 30 mL have collected, then the temperature rises sharply toward 100 °C as water starts to come over.
options: Liquid at acetone's temperature kept collecting past 10 mL.
Right: the first plateau ends near 30 mL.
60 mL is the total collected, including water.
The table shows only 60 mL collected.

why.correct: Between the plateaus, both liquids are vaporizing in a changing ratio, so the distillate is a mixture. A simple distillation does not cut perfectly between two liquids.
options: Right: the transition region holds both.
At 78 °C, well above acetone's boiling point, water is coming over too.
Water vaporizes at every temperature; at 78 °C both liquids are in the vapor.
Distillation is a physical separation; no reaction occurs.

why.correct: Sand has not dissolved, so its grains stay on filter paper while the salt water passes through.
options: Right: undissolved solid from a liquid.
Chromatography separates dissolved components, not a coarse solid.
Distillation would leave both sand and salt behind together.
Evaporation would leave salt mixed with the sand.

why.correct: A solution is mixed down to individual particles. Ions are about 10⁻¹⁰ m across, thousands of times smaller than filter pores, so they pass through with the water.
options: Right: dissolved particles pass through.
The ions pass through freely; they do not clog the filter.
Filtration is used for liquids all the time.
No reaction occurs with filter paper.

why.correct: Water has a measurable vapor pressure; the ions, held by strong ion-dipole and ionic attractions, do not enter the vapor. Condensing the vapor gives pure water.
options: Right: water vaporizes, ions stay behind.
Ions pass through filter paper.
Chromatography separates small samples of dissolved components; it does not yield pure water in bulk.
Dissolved salt does not settle out of a solution.

why.correct: The polar silica holds 1-propanol by hydrogen bonds; nonpolar hexane interacts only weakly with it and stays in the mobile phase, so it leaves first.
options: Right: weakest attraction to the stationary phase moves fastest.
A nonpolar solvent cannot hydrogen-bond; 1-propanol is held by the silica instead.
Separation follows attractions, not falling speed.
Size is not the main factor here; polarity is.

why.correct: Rf = 4.0 cm ÷ 12.5 cm = 0.32 (two significant figures, from 4.0).
Each physical method exploits a property that differs between components. The number of protons defines an element; physical separations do not change or use it.
options: Right: larger particles stay on the filter.
Right: stronger attraction to the stationary phase slows a component.
Right: the more volatile component vaporizes first.
Protons identify elements; physical separations neither use nor change them.
Separations follow attractions and size, not molar mass by itself.
The total mass says nothing about the parts of the mixture.

why.correct: The start line must sit above the solvent so the spots are not washed off, and the solvent front must be marked before it evaporates.
From 4 to 7 carbons the solubility drops from 7.7 to 0.17 g per 100 g water, each bar lower than the one before.
options: Right: a steady fall.
This reverses the trend.
The values span a factor of about 45.
The 6-carbon bar is lower than the 4- and 5-carbon bars.

why.correct: Each alcohol has one –OH that hydrogen-bonds to water. The growing carbon–hydrogen part attracts water only weakly, and fitting it in costs water–water hydrogen bonds, so solubility falls.
options: Right: the nonpolar part grows; the polar part does not.
Each of these alcohols has one –OH group, and –OH attracts water.
Dissolving depends on attractions, not on whether a molecule is heavy.
Carbon–hydrogen chains are nonpolar; longer chains make the molecule less polar overall.

why.correct: Each added carbon lowers the solubility; 1-octanol should fall below 1-heptanol's 0.17 g. (Its measured value is about 0.05 g per 100 g water.)
options: Miscibility belongs to the shortest alcohols, up to 3 carbons.
That is the 4-carbon value.
That range lies between the 6- and 7-carbon values; 8 carbons should be lower still.
Right: below the 7-carbon value.

why.correct: Like dissolves like: hexane is nonpolar, and the long chain of 1-hexanol interacts with it by dispersion forces of similar strength to those it replaces. In water the same chain disrupts strong hydrogen bonds.
options: Right: comparable attractions in hexane; a poor trade in water.
Hexane has no H on N, O or F and cannot hydrogen-bond.
Mixing does not break covalent bonds; the –OH stays on the molecule.
Water and hexane do not repel; water molecules just attract each other much more.

why.correct: The dissolved O₂ falls from 14.6 mg/L at 0 °C to 6.4 mg/L at 40 °C.
options: This reverses the trend in the table.
Right: lower at each higher temperature.
The values change by more than half.
Every value is lower than the one before.

why.correct: O₂ is held in water only by weak dipole-induced dipole and dispersion forces. Faster-moving molecules break away and escape into the air more readily.
options: Right: more kinetic energy, more escape.
O₂ cannot hydrogen-bond, and dissolving does not break the O=O bond.
O₂ is nonpolar at any temperature.
The O₂ partial pressure in air is 0.21 atm throughout.

why.correct: From 20 °C to 30 °C, dissolved O₂ falls from 9.1 to 7.6 mg/L. Warmer water holds less oxygen.
options: Right: less oxygen in warmer water.
Warmer water holds less oxygen, not more.
Temperature changes the amount dissolved, even with the same air.
At 40 °C the water still holds 6.4 mg/L.

why.correct: Raising the partial pressure from 0.21 atm to 1.00 atm makes O₂ molecules strike and enter the surface more often, so more dissolves (roughly 1.00/0.21 ≈ 4.8 times as much).
options: Right: higher partial pressure, more gas dissolved.
Pressure pushes gas into the liquid, not out.
Gas solubility depends on both temperature and pressure.
O₂ does not react with water.

why.correct: Hexane is nonpolar. I₂ is nonpolar too, so dispersion attractions between them are comparable to those each loses.
options: Right: like dissolves like.
Hexane cannot form ion-dipole attractions to replace NaCl's ionic bonds.
Sucrose's many –OH groups hydrogen-bond to each other; hexane offers nothing comparable.
Methanol hydrogen-bonds to itself; hexane cannot replace those attractions, though they do mix partly.

why.correct: Ethanol's –OH group forms hydrogen bonds with water about as strong as the ethanol–ethanol and water–water hydrogen bonds it replaces, and its two-carbon chain is too short to disrupt much.
options: Right: comparable hydrogen bonds formed.
Ethanol is a molecular compound and forms no ions.
Ethanol (46.07 g/mol) is much heavier than water (18.02 g/mol), and mass is not the cause.
Ethanol is polar, with an O–H group.

why.correct: Oil and water molecules attract by weak dispersion and dipole-induced dipole forces. Dissolving oil would cost water–water hydrogen bonds and give back much weaker attractions, so the water keeps to itself.
options: Right: a poor trade of attractions, not repulsion.
The attraction is weak, not strong; and size is not the main reason.
Oil is nonpolar, and polar molecules attract each other.
Oil is less dense and floats; density decides which layer is on top, not whether they mix.

why.correct: Like dissolves like. Water and methanol both hydrogen-bond. Hexane and octane are both nonpolar. Water with nonpolar hexane or CCl₄ separates into layers.
options: Right: both hydrogen-bond.
Right: both nonpolar, attracting by dispersion.
Hexane would cost water its hydrogen bonds.
CCl₄ is symmetric and nonpolar.

why.correct: Gas solubility rises with the gas's partial pressure and falls as temperature rises.

variables.name: The bottle is opened, so the CO₂ pressure above the soda falls to about 0.0004 atm
variables.why: Lower partial pressure of CO₂ means fewer molecules enter the liquid per second than leave, so CO₂ comes out as bubbles.

variables.name: The sealed bottle warms to 25 °C
variables.why: Warmer dissolved CO₂ molecules have more kinetic energy and escape the liquid more easily, so less stays dissolved.

variables.name: The sealed bottle is gently turned upside down and back at 5 °C
variables.why: Turning the bottle changes neither the temperature nor the CO₂ pressure, so the amount dissolved at equilibrium is unchanged.

why.correct: Polar or ionic solutes dissolve in polar solvents, and nonpolar in nonpolar, because the attractions formed match those broken.
options: Right: similar attractions.
Molar mass does not decide solubility.
Color has nothing to do with solubility.
Solids and gases dissolve in liquids all the time.

why.correct: Vitamin C's many –OH groups hydrogen-bond to water. Vitamin A's long nonpolar chain dominates its single –OH, so it dissolves in nonpolar fats instead.
options: Right: many polar groups versus a long nonpolar chain.
This reverses the two.
One –OH on a long chain is not enough, as the alcohol series shows.
Many molecular compounds, such as sugar, dissolve well in water.

why.correct: Infrared photons match the energy gaps between vibrational levels. The broad dip near 3,350 cm⁻¹ is in the O–H stretch range.
options: Right: IR excites vibrations; this one is O–H.
Electronic transitions need visible or UV photons, which carry more energy.
Rotation is changed by lower-energy microwaves.
Removing core electrons needs X-ray photons.

why.correct: The spectrum shows O–H (about 3,350), C–H (about 2,950) and C–O (about 1,050 cm⁻¹) absorptions, and no C=O near 1,700. Ethanol has all three bonds and no C=O.
options: Right: O–H, C–H and C–O, no C=O.
Acetone would show a strong C=O dip near 1,700 cm⁻¹, which is missing.
Hexane has no O–H or C–O bonds, so it would lack the dips at 3,350 and 1,050 cm⁻¹.
Water has no C–H bonds, so it would lack the dip near 2,950 cm⁻¹.

why.correct: Higher wavenumber means more energy per photon. So the gap between O–H vibrational levels is larger than the gap between C–O vibrational levels.
options: Right: higher wavenumber, larger energy gap.
The position, not the depth, gives the energy.
A higher energy gap means a faster, not slower, vibration.
Both are infrared absorptions, so both are vibrations.

why.correct: Acetone has a C=O bond (absorbs near 1,700 cm⁻¹) but no O–H bond, so the broad 3,350 cm⁻¹ dip disappears. IR spectra depend on the bonds, not only the elements.
options: Right: C=O appears; O–H disappears.
Different bonds give different absorptions even with the same elements.
Polar molecules absorb IR strongly.
Acetone is colorless; the instrument measures infrared here.

why.correct: The absorption peaks near 630 nm, in the red-orange part of the spectrum.
options: Absorption there is close to zero.
Absorption there is low.
Right: the peak of the curve.
Absorption has fallen far from its peak by 700 nm.

why.correct: We see the light that is not absorbed. Absorbing red-orange light near 630 nm leaves mostly blue and violet light to pass through, so the solution looks blue.
options: Right: the transmitted light sets the color.
A substance shows the color it does not absorb.
It absorbs little below 550 nm.
Absorbing a strong band of visible light gives a color.

why.correct: Visible photons carry enough energy to match electronic energy gaps, so an electron is promoted to an excited state.
options: Right: an electronic transition.
Vibrations are excited by lower-energy infrared light.
Rotation is excited by microwaves.
Visible light excites the electron; the molecule stays intact.

why.correct: 1,500 nm is infrared, longer than 630 nm, so each photon has less energy. Absorption needs a photon whose energy matches the gap; more photons of the wrong energy do not add up.
options: Right: energy must match the gap.
Longer wavelength means lower energy per photon.
Each photon must match the gap on its own; brightness adds photons, not energy per photon.
1,500 nm is infrared, not X-ray.

why.correct: Energy per photon rises as wavelength shrinks: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray.
Microwaves match rotational gaps, infrared vibrational gaps, and visible or ultraviolet light electronic gaps.
options: Right: microwaves match rotational gaps.
Right: infrared matches vibrational gaps.
UV photons carry far more energy than rotational gaps; they cause electronic transitions.
Visible light causes electronic transitions, not vibrations.
Right: UV matches electronic gaps.
Radio photons carry the least energy; removing core electrons needs X-rays.

why.correct: Microwave photons match the energy gaps of molecular rotation. Polar water molecules absorb them, rotate faster, and collide with neighbors, raising the temperature. The glass absorbs little.
options: Right: rotation of polar molecules.
Microwave photons carry less energy than visible photons and break no bonds.
Electronic transitions need visible or UV photons.
The glass absorbs little microwave energy and is warmed by the food instead.

why.correct: Of these, microwaves have the longest wavelengths (1 mm to 1 m) and the lowest energy per photon.
options: Ultraviolet is shorter than visible.
Visible light is 400–700 nm.
Infrared wavelengths are shorter than microwaves.
Right: 1 mm to 1 m.

why.correct: What matters is energy per photon. UV photons can promote electrons in molecules such as DNA and trigger reactions; IR photons only make bonds vibrate.
options: Right: energy per photon.
Light is not "hot"; heating comes from absorbed energy, and IR heats well.
IR from a heat lamp clearly reaches and warms the skin.
UV has a shorter wavelength than IR.

why.correct: A vibration absorbs infrared only if it changes the molecule's charge distribution. N₂'s symmetric stretch does not; CO₂ has bending and uneven stretching vibrations that do.
options: Right: N₂ does not absorb IR.
N₂ does not absorb IR, so its abundance does not make it a greenhouse gas.
Absorbing UV is not what traps heat radiated from Earth's surface.
IR causes vibrations, not electronic transitions.

why.correct: Infrared photons have energies that match vibrational gaps but fall far short of electronic gaps.
options: X-ray photons remove inner electrons.
UV photons match electronic gaps.
Visible photons match electronic gaps in colored substances.
Right: IR matches vibrational gaps.
Right: E = hc/λ with λ in meters.
This is hλ. Energy is E = hν = hc/λ, which falls as λ rises.
This is the energy of a mole of photons; one photon is 6.022 × 10²³ times smaller.
This used λ in nm. Convert first: 656.3 nm = 6.563 × 10⁻⁷ m.

why.correct: E = hc/λ, so the shortest wavelength carries the most energy. Line D, at 410.2 nm, comes from the largest energy drop.
options: Line A has the longest wavelength, so the smallest energy drop of the four.
Line B, at 486.1 nm, is a longer wavelength than two of the other lines.
Line C, at 434.0 nm, is longer than the 410.2 nm line.
Right: shortest wavelength, most energy.

why.correct: Electrons in an atom occupy fixed levels. A drop from one level to another emits a photon whose energy, and so wavelength, equals that gap exactly. A few gaps give a few lines.
options: Right: fixed levels, fixed photon energies.
A spectroscope spreads light out; it would show a continuous spectrum if one were emitted.
Atom size does not pick the colors; the gaps between levels do.
The light is emitted by the hot gas, not reflected.

why.correct: Doubling the wavelength from 300 nm to 600 nm halves the energy, from 6.62 to 3.31 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. E = hc/λ.
options: Right: E × λ is constant.
Energy falls as wavelength rises.
The drop gets smaller at longer wavelengths, so it is not linear.
The curve changes by a factor of four across the graph.

why.correct: E is proportional to 1/λ, so E(250)/E(750) = 750/250 = 3. No constants are needed.
λ = hc/E = (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ × 2.998 × 10⁸) / 4.97 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 400 nm. The graph shows 4.97 × 10⁻¹⁹ J at about 400 nm.
options: A 200 nm photon carries about twice the energy needed.
Right: the photon energy matches the gap.
A 600 nm photon carries only about two thirds of the energy needed.
An 800 nm photon carries about half the energy needed.

why.correct: A transition is caused by one photon of matching energy. A 700 nm photon carries hc/λ = 2.84 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Brightness changes the number of photons, not the energy of each.
options: Right: energy per photon decides.
Total energy is not what matters; each photon must match the gap.
Brightness does not change wavelength.
Red photons have less energy than the gap, not more.
Right: E = hc/λ with λ in meters.
This used λ in nm. Convert first: 589 nm = 5.89 × 10⁻⁷ m.
This is hλ. Energy is E = hc/λ.
This is a mole of photons, not one photon.

why.correct: E(one photon) = hc/λ = 3.3726 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Per mole: × 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 2.0310 × 10⁵ J/mol = 203.1 kJ/mol, which is 203 kJ/mol.
The energy of a photon is Planck's constant times its frequency.
options: Right: Planck's constant times frequency.
Energy falls as wavelength rises, so E is not proportional to λ.
That relates mass and energy; it is not on the equations sheet for this course.
This links wavelength and frequency, not energy.

why.correct: c = λν with c fixed, so doubling λ halves ν. E = hν, so the energy halves too.
options: Right: c fixed, E ∝ ν.
Longer waves have lower frequency and less energy.
E is proportional to ν, so they change together.
Doubling λ lowers ν, not raises it.

why.correct: Units first, then frequency, then energy per photon, then per mole, then kJ.
λ = hc/E = (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ × 2.998 × 10⁸) / 3.03 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 6.56 × 10⁻⁷ m = 656 nm. Only a photon of that energy matches the gap; photons of other energies are not absorbed for this transition.
options: Right: its energy equals the gap.
A 486 nm photon carries 4.09 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, more than the gap.
A 1,312 nm photon carries half the energy needed.
A 328 nm photon carries twice the energy needed.

why.correct: The line passes through the origin with slope 1.131 / 10.0 = 0.1131 per 10⁻⁵ M. c = 0.565 / 0.1131 = 4.996, so 5.00 × 10⁻⁵ M.
Any light lost at the cuvette walls is counted as absorbed by the sample. A higher absorbance read on the calibration line gives a higher concentration.
options: Right: extra absorbance, higher concentration.
Fingerprints block or scatter light; they do not let more through.
The beam passes through the walls, so anything on them affects the reading.
Path length is the inside width, which does not change.

why.correct: At λmax, ε is largest, so each change in concentration gives the largest change in absorbance, and small wavelength errors matter least.
options: Right: maximum absorbance, maximum sensitivity.
Water absorbs very little visible light; the blank removes small effects.
The dye looks blue because it absorbs orange-red light near 630 nm and transmits blue.
Violet, near 400 nm, is the shortest visible wavelength.

why.correct: The diluted solution is 5.00 × 10⁻⁵ M. The dilution factor is 50.0 / 10.0 = 5.00, so the original is 5.00 × 5.00 × 10⁻⁵ M = 2.50 × 10⁻⁴ M (M₁V₁ = M₂V₂).
options: This divides by the dilution factor instead of multiplying.
This is the diluted concentration, not the original.
This used the 40.0 mL of water added as V₁ (50.0/40.0); the volume of drink taken was 10.0 mL.
Right: multiply back by the dilution factor.

why.correct: A is proportional to c. Doubling c from 0.0500 to 0.1000 M doubles A: 2 × 0.592 = 1.184, so 1.18.
options: This halves instead of doubling.
This ignores the change in concentration.
Right: twice the concentration, twice the absorbance.
This quadruples; A is proportional to c, not c².

why.correct: A is proportional to the path length b. Same concentration as sample 1 but twice the path: 2 × 0.592 = 1.18.
options: This divides by 10 for no reason.
A longer path increases A; it does not halve it.
A longer path passes more absorbing ions, so A rises.
Right: twice the path, twice the absorbance.

why.correct: Without a blank, the instrument counts light lost to the cuvette and water as absorbed by copper(II). Each reading is too high, and c = A/(εb) is too high.
options: Right: a higher reading means a higher calculated concentration.
Extra absorbing material raises, not lowers, the reading.
The question states the cuvette and water absorb 0.015.
ε is a property of copper(II) at 810 nm; the error is in A.

why.correct: b is the path length, the distance light travels through the solution, usually 1.00 cm.
options: Right: usually 1.00 cm.
That is ε.
That is c.
The wavelength is chosen (λmax) but is not a variable in the equation.

why.correct: Pick the wavelength, zero with a blank, measure the standards, build the line, then measure the unknown.

A drop and a missed blank both add absorbance that is counted as the sample's. A shorter path lowers A, and over-dilution lowers the measured concentration; measuring everything at another wavelength only lowers sensitivity.
options: Right: extra light lost, higher A.
Right: the solvent's absorbance is added to every reading.
A shorter path gives a lower A and so a lower concentration.
Extra unrecorded dilution makes the calculated original concentration too low.
If standards and unknown use the same wavelength, the curve still works, just less sensitively.

why.correct: Absorption needs a photon whose energy matches a gap between levels. Sugar has no electronic transitions in the visible, so ε at 630 nm is about zero.
options: Right: ε is near zero at that wavelength.
Size does not decide absorption; matching energy gaps do.
Absorbed energy is mostly turned into heat, and here nothing is absorbed.
Even concentrated sugar solutions are colorless.

why.correct: At high absorbance, readings can fall below the Beer's-law line. Diluting the unknown into the range covered by good standards gives a reliable reading; multiplying by the dilution factor returns the original concentration.
options: Right: stay within the calibrated range.
The curve has already bent at high absorbance, so extending the line is unreliable there.
Its absorbance is higher, so its concentration is likely higher too.
Away from λmax the absorbance is lower, not higher, and the standards were not measured there.

why.correct: A = εbc. Only c and b (and ε, fixed for the dye at λmax) change A. Doubling c doubles A; the volume poured in and the brightness of the lamp do not appear in the equation, and a shorter path halves A.
